title: Retrieval Rhythm
user: A self-learner who wants to remember a small set of facts without learning an unfamiliar flashcard grading system.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asks why flashcard apps make the learner rate Good/Average/Bad instead of knowing how memorization is going.
A 22-reaction SRS improvement request asks for timer-based review, daily limits, more answer options, and better review controls.

recurrence: Two independent public requests; self-scoring and opaque review settings recur across mainstream SRS workflows. Severity is medium: the friction prevents a daily habit rather than merely inconveniencing an existing one.
current_workaround: Use Anki/Logseq buttons and guess a confidence rating, or abandon review after a few days.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki, RemNote, Logseq, and Mochi schedule cards, but make the learner operate the scheduler. The gap is a tiny recall practice that infers difficulty from a typed answer, latency, and retries while showing the reason for the next prompt.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA: create 20–100 prompt/answer items, answer by typing, receive transparent retry timing, and see a one-screen ‘due because…’ explanation. Non-goals: AI card generation, shared decks, and a full note app.
success_measure: In a four-week cohort, at least 35% of users with 20+ items complete review on 12 distinct days without changing a scheduling setting.
monetization: freemium — free single collection; paid local export, multiple collections, and advanced review history without charging for core memorization.
constraints: Local-first data and export; never claim the inferred score is a learning diagnosis; keyboard and screen-reader support; no copyrighted deck bundle.
why_distinct: It removes confidence buttons rather than cloning a card database or wrapping an LLM around Anki.

title: Knowledge Boundary Map
user: A self-learner who has consumed a topic but needs to distinguish recognition from an explanation they can actually produce.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Describes people collecting notes and content but being unable to tell what they understand deeply, only think they understand, or have missed.
A 565-reaction request proposes surfacing the next keyboard shortcut to learn from observed mouse use, rather than presenting a generic catalog.

recurrence: Two independent requests articulate the same metacognitive problem: learners need the next revealed gap, not more content. Severity is medium-high for independent study because false familiarity derails topic selection.
current_workaround: Keep an ever-growing notes system, reread material, or ask a friend/teacher to quiz them.
incumbents_and_gap: Obsidian, Notion, and Anki store or review knowledge; learning analytics tools are institution-heavy. None offers a lightweight, user-authored map that tests a claim, prerequisite, and counterexample before marking it understood.
smallest_useful_product: Static web app with a node map: add a claim and prerequisites, do a 90-second teach-back, then mark ‘explain’, ‘recognize’, or ‘blocked’ with a next probe. Non-goals: automatic truth checking, web scraping, and social feeds.
success_measure: At least 50% of activated users create five claims and revisit one previously overconfident claim within seven days.
monetization: one-time — a private, exportable personal tool has clear value without an ongoing inference bill.
constraints: Private-by-default browser storage; clearly label self-assessments; accessible diagram navigation; no claim of objectively measuring intelligence.
why_distinct: It is an explicit boundary-and-prerequisite rehearsal surface, not another knowledge base or generic quiz generator.

title: Concept Contrast Lab
user: A technical self-learner who can recognize terms but needs to retain causal, abstract concepts such as distributed-systems trade-offs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A system-design learner asks whether spaced repetition helps with deep understanding of abstract concepts or only rote memory.
A 16-reaction report says Logseq’s SRS produced implausible intervals and unsuitable reviews even with only about 200 cards, highlighting how generic scheduling can fail learning workflows.

recurrence: Two independent signals show the limit of fact-card repetition for concept learning. Severity is high for learners investing months in technical material but unable to transfer it.
current_workaround: Make cloze cards, reread books, or write informal notes and hope understanding survives.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki and Logseq optimize prompts and intervals; textbooks provide exposition. The gap is repeatable practice of contrast: when a rule applies, when it fails, and which counterexample changes the answer.
smallest_useful_product: PWA where users author a concept, a near-miss, a counterexample, and a transfer scenario; each session asks them to choose and justify the boundary. Non-goals: course hosting, LLM explanations, and automatic grading of open-ended essays.
success_measure: Among users completing six sessions on a concept, 60% correctly classify a new transfer scenario after seven days.
monetization: freemium — free personal labs; paid import/export templates and unlimited topic packs created by the user.
constraints: User-created content only; disclose that it practices reasoning but does not certify competence; keyboard-first interactions.
why_distinct: The unit of practice is a contrast and counterexample, not a front/back card or an AI answer chat.

title: Personal Vocab Loop
user: A language learner who wants words to survive in speech by practicing their own sentence and voice, not a generic streak.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A language-learning builder reports that learners struggle with vocabulary sticking long-term despite streaks, flashcards, and progress bars, and asks whether audio, personal sentences, immersion, writing, or teaching works.
A request to preserve per-user image and personal-note fields when updating shared Anki decks explains that personal memory aids are lost by deck-update workflows.

recurrence: Two independent requests identify retention and personalization as the problem, not starting motivation. Severity is high for serious language learners because forgotten active vocabulary makes progress feel fake.
current_workaround: Use Duolingo or Anki plus separate notes, record voice memos, and manually protect personal annotations during deck changes.
incumbents_and_gap: Duolingo, Anki, Memrise, and Migaku offer courses or cards. They rarely make a learner repeatedly retrieve a personally useful phrase, listen to their own recording, and keep that personal context portable.
smallest_useful_product: Offline mobile PWA: capture word, personal sentence, optional 10-second recording, and context tag; prompt active recall and replay on a transparent schedule. Non-goals: machine translation, public decks, and gamified streaks.
success_measure: After 21 days, at least 40% of users with 30 saved phrases complete a blind spoken or typed recall check for 70% of sampled phrases.
monetization: one-time — voice/context data stays on-device and the core value does not require a content subscription.
constraints: Explicit microphone permission; local encrypted export; no children’s-data targeting; user owns recordings and examples.
why_distinct: It is a personal phrase-and-voice retention loop, not another language course, dictionary, or streak mechanic.

title: Math Tooling Notebook
user: An adult returning to mathematics who needs hands-on fluency with graphs, symbolic notation, estimates, and checks before tackling a formal course.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asks for a mathematics equivalent of MIT’s practical ‘Missing Semester’ course rather than another conventional textbook sequence.
The 244-reaction graphing-mode proposal frames high-school algebra as a STEM gateway and calls out its high failure rate, validating demand for approachable mathematical tooling.

recurrence: Two independent signals, including a high-reaction tool request, point to mathematical practice tooling being a missing layer between explanations and coursework. Severity is high for returners blocked before advanced study.
current_workaround: Bounce among Desmos, WolframAlpha, calculators, videos, and paper notes without a guided tool-literacy sequence.
incumbents_and_gap: Desmos, GeoGebra, WolframAlpha, and textbooks are powerful but assume tool choice and workflow knowledge. The gap is short, reproducible ‘inspect / estimate / graph / verify’ drills that teach when each tool is appropriate.
smallest_useful_product: Static web notebook with 20 tool-literacy drills, an embedded function plotter, scratchpad, estimation reveal, and local progress. Non-goals: a CAS, full curriculum, adaptive AI tutor, or graded certificates.
success_measure: At least 50% of new users complete five drills and correctly choose graph, table, estimate, or algebraic check on a six-question transfer quiz.
monetization: free — a useful acquisition utility with no account burden; later paid printable instructor packs are optional.
constraints: Use permissively licensed math-rendering/plotting libraries; WCAG-friendly graph alternatives; no exam-prep claims.
why_distinct: It teaches the workflow around math tools rather than competing as a graphing calculator or a content course.

title: Linux Learning Station
user: A parent or teacher setting up an older shared Linux computer for 5–10-year-olds who needs offline, age-progressive learning activities without accounts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent using GCompris for a five-year-old asks what comes next, saying free Linux educational games seem limited for older children.
A college Python instructor describes per-user installation as a classroom blocker and needs a ready-to-use environment for 50 students at login.

recurrence: Two independent classroom/home setup requests expose a deployment problem alongside the content gap. Severity is medium-high where accounts, app installs, and weak connectivity exclude devices from use.
current_workaround: Install assorted apps one by one, rely on browser sites, or default to GCompris past its intended level.
incumbents_and_gap: GCompris, TuxMath, and web learning sites exist, but discovery and age progression are fragmented. The gap is a single offline launch page with a small curated progression and no child account.
smallest_useful_product: Installable offline PWA with six original, local mini-activities (patterns, keyboarding, logic, spelling, number sense, creative drawing), parent-configured age bands, and printable progress code. Non-goals: a content marketplace, cloud profiles, and licensed game aggregation.
success_measure: In five home/classroom pilots, an adult can install and start a child activity in under five minutes without creating an account; children return for three sessions in one week.
monetization: one-time — schools and families can buy an offline bundle without tracking children or managing subscriptions.
constraints: COPPA/GDPR-K by design: no telemetry, chat, ads, or external links in child mode; original or permissively licensed assets only; work on low-end Chromium.
why_distinct: It solves local deployment and age progression with original micro-activities rather than cloning a commercial kids’ platform.

title: Arithmetic Steps
user: An elementary teacher or parent who wants children to see and manipulate the intermediate structure of arithmetic rather than memorize answer snapshots.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asks whether people learned arithmetic as procedures or ‘snapshots’ and whether math education should make the inner steps more visible.
A 23-reaction request from a student who uses Mermaid for school asks for array/linked-list diagrams because lectures need visual structure.

recurrence: Two independent requests point to the value of making hidden steps visual. Severity is high when early answer memorization prevents later explanation and transfer.
current_workaround: Use worksheets, physical counters, or video demonstrations that cannot record the child’s own decomposition choices.
incumbents_and_gap: Khan Academy, SplashLearn, and digital manipulatives offer practice, but many optimize speed or correct answers. The gap is a deliberately slow, replayable trail of ‘make ten’, split, regroup, and compare decisions.
smallest_useful_product: Offline web game for addition/subtraction to 100: drag counters/ten-frames, narrate each transformation in plain language, replay an attempt, and generate a parent/teacher discussion card. Non-goals: leaderboard, timed drills, AI grading, or a full K–12 curriculum.
success_measure: After three sessions, 70% of sampled children can explain one correct decomposition in words or by replaying their trail, not merely select the total.
monetization: free — the small, no-account learning utility should be usable in homes and classrooms; optional print pack can fund maintenance.
constraints: No child identifiers; accessible color and non-drag input alternatives; teacher-reviewed pedagogy; original visual assets.
why_distinct: The product preserves a child’s reasoning trail for conversation; it is not a speed-drill or answer-checking math clone.

title: Note Rehearsal Router
user: A self-learner with a markdown note graveyard who wants a saved idea to become one concrete recall, solve, or explain action.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 68-comment request describes Obsidian notes and links becoming a ‘graveyard of good intentions’ and seeks surfacing material with a concrete next action.
An 18-reaction request asks to exclude raw-note folders from flashcard search until notes are ready, showing the need to separate capture from rehearsal.

recurrence: At least two independent workflows report capture-to-action failure; the HN post has substantial discussion. Severity is high for heavy note takers because organizing cost displaces learning.
current_workaround: Over-tag notes, periodically review folders, manually copy selected text to Anki, or let unfinished notes accumulate.
incumbents_and_gap: Obsidian, Notion, Readwise, and Obsidian-to-Anki handle capture or export. The unresolved gap is a local triage lane that asks what kind of action a note deserves before it becomes a card, task, or archive.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension plus local markdown folder watcher: present one untriaged note at a time and create exactly one local ‘recall’, ‘solve’, ‘teach’, ‘do’, or ‘archive’ ticket. Non-goals: semantic search, autonomous task creation, cloud sync, and LLM summaries.
success_measure: For users importing 30+ notes, 30% convert at least ten notes into completed rehearsal actions within 14 days.
monetization: one-time — local markdown workflow and no hosted inference make a durable purchase reasonable.
constraints: Filesystem permission and data stay local; markdown parsing must be non-destructive; clear uninstall/export; do not read private pages without explicit opt-in.
why_distinct: It routes a note into a deliberately chosen learning action, not an AI summary, second-brain search engine, or automatic flashcard factory.

title: Code Lesson Checkpoints
user: A remote programming tutor who needs to see a learner’s runnable milestones and misconceptions without constantly taking over their screen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A prospective 1:1 coding-teaching tool asks tutors which remote tools they use and what is most frustrating about Zoom, Replit, and VS Code Live Share.
A 45-reaction Live Share request says collaborators need to run a project on their own machines; otherwise they rely on video streaming to share the project.

recurrence: Two independent remote-coding workflows identify the same visibility/control trade-off. Severity is high in paid tutoring: screen-share time is expensive and hides learner process.
current_workaround: Use Zoom plus screen share, send zip files, share control in Live Share, or ask the learner to narrate terminal output.
incumbents_and_gap: Zoom, Replit, VS Code Live Share, and Codespaces provide communication or shared editing. The gap is a lesson-specific checkpoint record: learner-run command, result, short reflection, and teacher response without remote control.
smallest_useful_product: VS Code extension and tiny backend: instructor defines shell/test checkpoints; student runs locally and shares only command status, selected output, and an optional note; teacher sees a timeline. Non-goals: remote desktop, surveillance recording, automated grading, and code generation.
success_measure: In ten tutor sessions, teachers identify the first blocked checkpoint in under two minutes and rate it more useful than requesting another screen share in at least 70% of sessions.
monetization: freemium — free individual tutor/student pair; paid small-team history and roster controls finance secure relay infrastructure.
constraints: Never upload source by default; redact environment variables and cap output; consent indicators for both parties; FERPA/GDPR-ready deletion and access controls.
why_distinct: It records learner-owned execution evidence rather than being another browser IDE, video call, or AI coding tutor.

title: Rubric Comment Queue
user: A teacher who must give humane, consistent writing feedback to many students while retaining control over every comment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asks how teachers are handling writing feedback at scale and explicitly contrasts tools with manual feedback.
An assessment-platform feature request explains that accommodations require individualized assessment handling beyond a simple extension, underscoring feedback/marking workflow complexity.

recurrence: Two independent educator/assessment signals show that feedback volume and individual treatment collide. Severity is high because rushed comments affect student learning and teacher workload.
current_workaround: Copy/paste comment banks in documents, use rubrics in an LMS, or hand off first-pass feedback to opaque AI tools.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Classroom, Canvas, Turnitin, Writable, and AI graders offer grading workflows, but they are often LMS-bound or auto-generate prose. The gap is a local-first queue that reuses teacher-authored feedback patterns while preserving a review-and-edit step for every student.
smallest_useful_product: Web app: import plain text or paste excerpts, attach a rubric criterion, choose/edit a teacher-written comment block, add one personal next step, then export CSV/clipboard. Non-goals: essay scoring, plagiarism detection, student profiling, and automatic AI feedback.
success_measure: In a 30-submission pilot, a teacher completes first-pass feedback 30% faster than their baseline while independently rating at least 90% of comments as specific enough to send.
monetization: subscription — small recurring teams need encrypted storage, class rosters, and audit/deletion controls.
constraints: FERPA/GDPR: minimal student data, deletion controls, encryption, no model training on submissions; accessibility and accommodation-safe workflow; teacher remains decision maker.
why_distinct: It accelerates teacher-authored feedback selection and personalization, rather than being a thin LLM essay grader.

title: Exam Bridge
user: A returning exam candidate who needs a compact concept-to-past-question bridge for a stated syllabus, before committing to many textbooks or paid test prep.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A GATE Electronics candidate wants one guide that covers the syllabus before past papers and mocks, specifically rejecting a return to disconnected individual textbooks.
A curriculum proposal asks OSSU to reconsider high-school math sequencing, describing prerequisite order as a persistent problem for self-directed learners.

recurrence: Two independent curriculum requests show the same prerequisite-navigation pain. Severity is high for adult candidates with limited study time and a high-stakes exam date.
current_workaround: Download a syllabus PDF, gather textbooks/videos, make a spreadsheet, and discover prerequisite gaps only after failing old questions.
incumbents_and_gap: Coaching platforms, YouTube, official syllabi, and question banks offer material. The gap is a user-owned map linking each syllabus bullet to a short prerequisite refresher and an openly licensed or user-entered past-question reference without republishing exam content.
smallest_useful_product: Static web planner: paste a syllabus outline, select confidence per topic, get a manually curated prerequisite checklist and study sequence, and attach personal links/question IDs. Non-goals: hosting copyrighted questions, promising pass rates, proctoring, or AI-generated lectures.
success_measure: At least 60% of activated candidates build a plan with ten mapped topics and return to update confidence after one practice session within a week.
monetization: freemium — free planner and export; paid reusable planning templates for permitted exam domains.
constraints: Do not distribute copyrighted coaching notes or test questions; clearly attribute official syllabus sources; no claims of affiliation with exam authorities.
why_distinct: It is a prerequisite-and-practice navigation layer, not a copied question bank, course marketplace, or AI cram chatbot.

title: Branching Problem Circle
user: A volunteer math-circle leader running a small group of curious children who needs to reveal divergent solution paths without turning the session into test prep.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A prospective leader wants a 6–8-child math ‘thinking lab’ around olympiad-style problems, depth, failed approaches, and alternative strategies rather than grades or speed.
An interactive-lesson feature request asks software to follow variation branches rather than only the main line so learners can encounter and respond to alternative moves.

recurrence: Two independent interactive-learning requests favor meaningful branching over a single prescribed path. Severity is medium-high: group leaders need usable structure but should not need formal-teacher tooling.
current_workaround: Use a whiteboard, shared slides, paper handouts, and ad hoc discussion; promising wrong approaches vanish after the meeting.
incumbents_and_gap: AoPS, Desmos Classroom, Kahoot, and chess lessons offer content or polling. The gap is a facilitator-led, small-group branching board where failed approaches are productive artifacts and reveal timing is deliberate.
smallest_useful_product: Offline-capable facilitator web app: author one problem, add up to six approach branches, collect anonymous ‘try this’ votes, reveal hints/branches, and export a one-page session recap. Non-goals: public child profiles, rankings, standardized-test banks, and AI solution generation.
success_measure: In five pilot circles, facilitators run a 45-minute session without switching tools and at least 75% of participating children submit a rationale or alternative path.
monetization: one-time — small groups need a low-admin local tool; optional facilitator template pack can be sold separately.
constraints: No public sharing or child accounts; facilitators supply rights-cleared problems; accessible keyboard voting and printable fallback.
why_distinct: It preserves and sequences competing approaches for a live small group, not another quiz, worksheet library, or generic online whiteboard.
